title: Japanese verb tenses
summary: Japanese has two tenses, non-past and past. "Is doing" is a white engine, て + いる, and time words follow a simple に rule.

blocks.text: So far every verb has been in its plain dictionary form. Japanese has just **two tenses**: the **non-past** (the dictionary form) and the **past**. There is no separate present and no separate future.
The non-past is not a present tense

Think of the non-past like English "I eat at six": it covers habits, facts, and above all **things that will happen**. So 犬が食べる most naturally means "The dog will eat." The past is made by changing the ending: 食べる becomes 食べた.

blocks.en: The dog will eat. (or: The dog eats.)

blocks.text: For something happening **right now**, Japanese uses **いる**, the "to be" for people and animals, together with the **て-form** of the verb. 食べて is a **white engine**: a verb that cannot pull the train alone but adds information to the real engine, いる. (You will learn how to make the て-form in the next lesson.)
犬が食べている。 The dog is eating.

A **relative** time word (relative to now: 明日 tomorrow, 今日 today, 昨日 yesterday) goes at the start of the sentence with **no particle**. An **absolute** time (a day of the week, a clock time) takes **に**. A good rule of thumb: if English would say "on / at / in", Japanese uses に.

blocks.jp: 明日（私が）ケーキを食べる。
火曜日に（私が）ケーキを食べる。

items: The non-past usually points to the **future** or to a habit.
**て + いる** says an action is **in progress**.
Relative time (明日, 今日): **no particle**. Absolute time (火曜日, 六時): **に**.

questions.instruction: How many tenses does a plain Japanese verb have?
questions.note: Non-past and past. The non-past covers present habits and the future.

questions.instruction: What does this most naturally say?
options: The dog will eat (or eats as a habit)
The dog is eating right now
questions.note: The non-past leans toward the future.

questions.instruction: How do you say "The dog is eating (right now)"?
questions.note: て-form + いる shows an action in progress.

questions.instruction: In 犬が食べている, which part is the engine?
questions.note: いる pulls the train. 食べて is a white engine that adds what the dog is doing.

questions.instruction: Which time word needs the particle に?
questions.note: A clock time is absolute, so it takes に. 明日, 今日 and 昨日 are relative: no particle.
An absolute time word takes に.

questions.prompt: Japanese has a separate future-tense ending.
questions.note: The non-past form is used for the future as well.

questions.instruction: How do you make the plain past of 食べる?
questions.note: Drop る and add た.

questions.instruction: Tap the relative time word (no particle needed)
questions.note: 明日 is relative to now, so it takes no particle.

questions.instruction: What does て + いる show?
questions.note: さくらが歩いている: Sakura is walking.

questions.instruction: Where does the relative time word 明日 go?
options: At the start, with no particle
questions.note: 明日（私が）ケーキを食べる。
